query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: DFT-guided doping of the near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst with Co, Ni, Bi, and Sn will modify the Pt(111) surface sites to enhance low-temperature oxidation, improve resistance to H2O and NO poisoning, and sustain durability under automotive aging conditions without increasing platinum-group-metal loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst featuring Pt-based active sites.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled amounts of Co, Ni, Bi, and Sn dopants into the Pt(111) facets of the catalyst based on DFT guidance.
generation.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust conditions including transient operation and low temperatures (below 150 °C) with exposure to water vapor and NO, alongside accelerated aging protocols mimicking vehicle lifetime mileage.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified Pt(111) surface sites where the dopants alter the local electronic structure.
generation.mechanism: The dopants are expected to tune the d-band center of Pt, lowering the activation energies for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation while reducing the binding strength of poisoning species (H2O and NO), thus leading to better catalytic performance and durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the doped catalyst should exhibit a lower light-off temperature (indicating enhanced activity), maintained activity in the presence of poisoning agents, and reduced performance degradation after accelerated aging.
generation.baseline: The unmodified near-equiatomic multi-principal-element catalyst without Co, Ni, Bi, and Sn doping.
generation.boundary: These improvements are expected under low-temperature, transient exhaust conditions with realistic levels of H2O and NO and over the catalyst’s operational lifetime equivalent to real-driving emission studies.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentrations and spatial distribution of the dopants remain to be precisely determined, and effects on long-term mechanical stability under repeated thermal cycles need further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one set with DFT-guided doping of Pt(111) sites using Co, Ni, Bi, and Sn and a control set without doping. Subject both sets to identical simulated exhaust conditions featuring low-temperature operation (below 150 °C), controlled introduction of poisoning species (H2O and NO), and accelerated aging protocols that mimic a full vehicle lifetime.
measurements: Light-off temperature for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation
Catalytic activity measurements in the presence of H2O and NO
Performance retention after accelerated aging cycles (e.g., before and after thousands of thermal cycles)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped catalyst does not demonstrate a measurable reduction in light-off temperature (e.g., a decrease of at least ~10 °C), fails to show improved activity in the presence of poisons, or does not retain significantly better performance after aging compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

chosen.approach: DFT-guided doping of Pt(111) with Co, Ni, Bi, Sn
